AI for Financial Services
AI for Financial ServicesMade by Katrina LiAllocator live site ↗
Financial services · Katrina Li

I built a harness that does a five-day stock ramp in under 20 minutes. Then I made it cheap enough to run on every desk in finance.

You give it one ticker. It returns a full hedge-fund-grade model in Excel and an initiation deck. This is how it works, how I trained it, how routing across Claude’s models keeps the cost down, and how the same method carries Claude across finance: investment banking, private markets, and FP&A and the back office.

Why this matters: Claude already has the finance agents, plugins and connectors. The gap now is deployment, from months to days, desk by desk. This is the method I’d bring: one narrow workflow a desk can check, house rules captured as skills, and Opus spent only where an error spreads.

01 · The problem

Ramping a new stock costs an analyst about a week before they can have a view.

You read the filings, rebuild the history, build revenue and costs from the bottom up, value it, and write it up. At a hedge fund that is roughly five days of work, about $6,000–7,500 fully loaded, before anyone has made a decision.

Same ramp, two ways

Elapsed5.0 days

What the PM needs

A view, a number, and a reason to trade. The spreadsheet is the cost of getting there, not the product.

Where the week goes

Most of it is mechanical: reading, re-keying twelve quarters, wiring formulas, formatting. The judgment calls take hours, not days.

Why it matters

A five-day ramp caps how many names a team can cover. At twenty minutes the limit becomes judgment, which is where analysts should spend their time.

03 · How I built it

I trained it the way banks train analysts: show good work, mark up the drafts, repeat.

I picked 10–20 names per sector that I know well, paired each with its filings and the model I would want to see, and wrote the house rules into guide tabs. Supervised learning taught the shape of a good model. Reinforcement learning taught judgment: every draft was marked right or wrong, with the comment a senior analyst would leave.

The training loop

Every draft is graded, and every grade is a reward

You are the reviewer. Each call becomes a reward.

Two stages of training

Stage 1 · supervisedImitate the models I trust

Filings in, preferred model out, for 10–20 names per sector. It learns tab structure, driver layout, colour coding and the order a reviewer reads in.

Stage 2 · reinforcementGrade drafts, keep what scores

Rewards come from checks a script can run (the balance sheet balances, the cash flow ties, every hardcode has a source) plus my right/wrong calls and comments.

04 · The Allocator

Running one frontier model on every step is the most expensive way to be wrong.

A ramp is dozens of steps. A few need real judgment, like how to split NVIDIA's revenue or which terminal growth rate to use. Most are reading and reformatting. So the harness breaks the job down, scores each step by how much damage an error would do downstream, and sends it to the cheapest model that clears the bar.

Frontier models are the CPUFew, expensive, branching decisions

What matters in this company, how to split the work, how to segment revenue, which assumption sets the answer. Claude Opus 5.5 decides. Where the blast radius is widest, GPT-5 re-derives the same claim from the same evidence: a second family cannot repeat the first one’s blind spot the way a model checking its own work does.

Cheap and open models are the GPUWide, parallel, repetitive work

Read 600 pages of filings, normalize XBRL, rebuild twelve quarters, format to house style. Claude Sonnet and GPT-5 mini build and draft; Llama 4 Maverick does the bulk reading on the bank’s own GPUs, so filings and anything market-sensitive never leave its network.

Route the NVDA ramp

Per-step cost and tokens from the recorded dispatch run in my paper, measured on my original multi-model mix across Claude, GPT and open-weight models. Reliability per step and the rework charge (two analyst hours at $150 when a run fails review) are my modeling assumptions.

The execution ledger

Every claim is a node. Node size and the number inside are its blast radius: how many later results break if it is wrong. Click any node.

What this means in product: routing by blast radius across vendors — open weights read inside the bank’s own cloud, Sonnet and GPT-5 mini build, Opus decides, GPT-5 re-derives the widest claims, a person signs — makes the frontier affordable exactly where it changes the answer, so a bank can run it on every name and every close. Putting the verifier in a different family is the part a single-vendor stack cannot buy: a model checking its own work repeats its own blind spots.
05 · Research · Allocating Intelligence (working paper, July 2026)

On top of the harness: a control plane for a fund's agent workforce.

A fund will soon run hundreds of background agents. Someone has to decide which ones get budget, which outputs get checked, and which agents have earned more autonomy. That is portfolio management, applied to agents. The paper lays out how.

Errors compound on long tasks

36.6% end-to-end
99.0%
100

A 99%-reliable agent finishes a 100-step task about 37% of the time. You cannot buy 99.9% everywhere, so buy it where an error spreads.

Capability 1Causal execution, not a log

Every claim is a node linked to its evidence and to everything downstream. A log says what happened in order. The graph says what depends on what.

Capability 2Verification follows blast radius

Blast radius is risk-weighted reachability. Choosing what to check is a minimum-cost cut: verify the few nodes that separate likely errors from the final call. Banks hold capital against risk-weighted assets the same way.

Capability 3Durable learning

When a model, prompt or tool changes, only the affected nodes are marked dirty and re-derived, like a build system recompiling what changed.

Earned autonomy

An agent starts on probation. Verified milestones expand its budget and scope. A failed verification cuts the budget and restores the human gate.

Cost per verified outcome

75–86% lower

Modeled at July 2026 list prices across 5–120 step tasks. On an all-frontier run a late error forces a full re-run; the ledger contains the failure and re-derives only what broke.

Applied to a hedge fund: earnings night

Twelve covered names report after the close. Agents update every model. The ledger only escalates the estimate changes that move a recommendation, so the PM reviews a short queue instead of twelve models.

    07 · FP&A, accounting & bank back office

    Where I’d start with banks: earn the context through one workflow, instead of asking anyone to write it down.

    The full adoption plan for the back office, as a live demo: the method, who to enter through, three narrow entry workflows you can click through, and where to start.

    Claude for the Back OfficeFP&A, accounting and bank back office · adoption plan and live demo · Katrina Li
    The method

    Don’t ask employees to write context. Earn it through one workflow that unlocks the next, and save it as skills as you go.

    Back-office work is reconciliation: every system has to tell the same story, and every number gets checked again. The logic for that lives in people’s heads. Nobody will write it down, but they will grant access when a task needs it and answer a yes/no question in five seconds.

    Old way: ask staff to write skills or a full guide

    • It takes hours on top of the month-end close.
    • It goes stale within a quarter.
    • It makes the writer replaceable.

    So it never gets written.

    New way: grant access, answer yes or no

    ClaudeYou’ve cut Q4 revenue by 20% in each of the past 3 years. Is that because enterprise implementations slip into Q1? Do it again?
    FP&A leadYes, only for enterprise contracts signed after September.
    ClaudeSaved as a rule (owner: you). To check implementation dates I need read-only CRM access. OK?
    Rule saved · owner: FP&A leadAccess asked: CRM, read-onlyStaff time: 5 seconds

    The method, in order

    1Pick a narrow workflow that wins a 30-minute live demo
    provable against their own outputrepeats monthlya pain they care about

    The trick: narrow, but impossible to finish without the client’s reconciliation logic (so Claude asks) and other systems’ data (so Claude requests access).

    2Enter through the most motivated team: management accounting

    They are judged on business insight, not GAAP detail. AI doing the grind faster only makes them look better.

    3Through that one workflow, earn access to the rest

    To explain any driver, the team grants read-only access to FP&A, accounting and controller data, one request at a time, each with a live reason.

    4Watch, learn and update as the work happens

    Every yes/no answer becomes a rule with an owner. Every repeated pattern becomes a skill. Past months get replayed before a change goes live.

    Why management accounting is the right way in

    1 · Their goal is operational insight

    • Travel +18% on flat headcount → tighten the travel policy
    • Marketing +$5m from 3 events that brought no new leads → cut them
    • Cost per loan +12% in one unit → reprice or restaff

    2 · Natural motivation, no fear

    • They are judged on the conclusions, and they sign off.
    • Claude does the 80-report grind; they present sharper insights, faster.
    • It makes them look smarter. Accounting staff, by contrast, fear replacement.

    3 · Their work pulls in everyone’s data

    • To explain any driver, Claude needs accounting’s ledger, sub-ledgers and close files, and treasury’s cash data.
    • Example: the travel spike → read access to the expense sub-ledger → Claude learns how accounting codes and accrues travel.
    Result: one team’s monthly report becomes the door into accounting and treasury workflows, without anyone writing documentation.

    Where to start

    Start where the gap is biggest and where a way in already exists.

    Second-tier banks hire Goldman-trained people and want Goldman-grade control, but they can’t build Goldman’s systems. So the work is still manual, and that is the gap.

    Main focus

    How in: the CFO sponsors; we enter through the head of management accounting with workflow 1 (titles: Head of FP&A, Management Reporting, Corporate Planning).

    Cluster 2 · a separate motion

    Big 4 quality of earnings, PwC first

    Why: a quality-of-earnings review comes with every deal and mirrors bank work. It’s a fixed fee (about $150K–$500K, up to ~$1M on complex deals), so every hour saved is margin.

    Way in: PwC launched an Office of the CFO practice built on Claude (May 2026). KPMG (May 2026) and Deloitte (Oct 2025) also have Anthropic alliances.

    Claude asks“You added back $2m of ‘one-time’ consulting three years running. Still one-time?”

    Compounds: each deal sharpens the firm’s own review playbook.

    Cluster 3 · channels, checked

    Accenture, Cognizant, InfosysUseClaude partners already inside banks’ back offices.
    GenpactHarderIts finance agents are built with Google Cloud (May 2026).
    PilotLaterSmall-business books, not banks.
    BasisRivalBuilt on OpenAI models. Works with ~30% of the top 25 accounting firms; valued at $1.15B (Feb 2026).
    FragmentSkipAcquired by Sierra (Apr 2026).

    Months 0–3Demos of workflows 1–3 → SMBC and Mizuho pilots, plus PwC quality of earnings and one outsourcer.
    Months 3–6Earn access to more workflows in each pilot. Package the skills owners have confirmed.
    Months 6–12Roll the packaged workflows out to more Cluster 1 banks, then through outsourcers and the Big 4.
